newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Deng death largely discounted as Asia stocks open.
newsitem.headline: Deng death largely discounted as Asia stocks open.

text.p: Stocks in China plunged and were expected to be volatile in Hong Kong, Taiwan and Singapore markets on Thursday after news that China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping had died, but many other Asian markets remain focused on domestic considerations.
Shanghai shares opened nearly all 10 percent limit-down on Thursday in reaction to Deng's death, which was announced overnight.
"For the first time ever foreign markets will look to Shenzhen and Shanghai reactions as a benchmark rather than the other way around," said Peter Churchouse, regional strategist at Morgan Stanley.
Market-watchers in Hong Kong said there could be a moderate reaction but that any move is likely to be temporary.
"Probably to a large extent it has been discounted because of the rumours of the past week," said Howard Gorges, a director at South China Brokerage.
"I think...a kneejerk reaction is expected with perhaps the market dropping three or four hundred points," he added.
The key Hang Seng Index ended off 3.38 points, or 0.03 percent, at 13,106.32 on Wednesday.
Some analysts believe investor attention will be more focused on the reaction within China itself on Thursday.
Dealers said Singapore shares could weaken initially in response to the news, but that any impact would be limited.
But in Tokyo traders were not anticipating much reaction.
"I don't think there will be an impact on stocks, and foreign exchange looks unaffected," said Yasuo Ueki, a general manager at Nikko Securities.
U.S. markets showed little reaction to the news, which came while they were open.
"This news has been largely discounted over the last several years," one market economist said.

Another analyst noted that Deng had already retired from politics in 1993 and that Communist Party chief Jiang Zemin had been carefully positioned to assume the top leadership in anticipation of Deng's death.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ended off 47.33 points at 7,020.13 on Wednesday.
The dollar rose on the news but finished off highs at 1.6980 marks and 124.55 yen, compared with 1.6855 marks and 123.85 yen, respectively, on Tuesday.
The dollar weakened slightly against the yen in early Tokyo trading, but dealers expect the currency will attract buying if it falls to 123 yen.
Tokyo shares rose, with the key Nikkei 225-share index up 230.09 points at the opening, or 1.24 percent, to 18,829.21.
Traders said the market benefitted from a newspaper report that the Japanese government may use more public funds to solve Japan's bad loan problem, which has hurt bank stocks.
"Brokers may be inclined to stay on the sidelines until the Hong Kong market opens and see its reaction to Deng's death," another broker in Tokyo said.
In Taiwan, share prices fell slightly early before recovering.
The index opened 19.14 points or 0.25 percent lower at 7,637.71 but after 15 minutes the index defied expectations to rise 33.25 points.
"This shows how investors have been expecting Deng's death for such a long time that it's almost an anticlimax when it happens," said Lin Long-hsien, analyst for United Securities.
Other brokers said the index already had reacted to the news because rumours on Deng's failing health had hit the market several days ago.
Taiwan's finance minister, Paul Chiu, said he did not expect the market to plunge because of Deng's death.
"The news of Deng's deteriorating health has been circulated for a long time, the day (of his death) is expected," Chiu told the state-funded Central News Agengy.
"I believe the stock market will not plunge," he said.
Australian shares opened lower in line with the drop on Wall Street and a cautious mood ahead of the release of corporate earnings. Traders said Deng's death was not a market factor.
The All Ordinaries share index was off 9.5 points, or 0.38 percent at 2,481.5.
Similarly, in New Zealand, stocks were weak at midsession, with Deng's death having no impact on trading. The market was off 7.64 points, or 0.33 percent, at 2321.71.
